story.headline: Markets now expect a Bank of Canada hike next week after Macklem warned on oil-driven inflation. A surprise drop in UK unemployment lifted the pound before Wednesday's inflation test.

reads.policy: Canada and New Zealand jumped the queue: markets now expect both to hike next week, joining the Bank of England in November. The Fed, ECB and BoJ are still waiting until December. Currencies whose banks are about to act, like the loonie, kiwi and pound, have the rate edge for now.
reads.growth: Britain's job market turned out firmer than feared, which gives the Bank of England less reason to hold back. China kept its lending rates steady after its growth beat, so no extra boost is coming. In the US, housing is the weak spot, but it isn't changing the Fed's plans.
reads.inflation: Energy is working its way through the system: German factory prices rose at the fastest pace in three and a half years. Canada's central bank now says it will act on where inflation is heading, not where it is today. That forward-looking stance is what moved rate bets this week.
reads.risk: Asia was calm. A US denial that it struck Iran took some heat out of Monday's scare, though Iran sticks to its account. France's unrest is still the main stress in Europe, so safe havens keep a floor without a fresh push.
reads.tot: Oil kept its supply premium because tankers still aren't moving through the Gulf at normal levels. That keeps helping exporters like Canada and costing importers like Japan and the euro area. It also keeps US yields high, which is weighing on gold.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar just as markets swung to expect a Bank of Canada hike, which leaves those bets exposed. They are also betting against the kiwi as hike odds there rise. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors disagree.
reads.fiscal: France votes today on the revenue half of its budget, with curfews in several cities and its borrowing costs at their widest gap to Germany in at least two weeks. A clean pass would ease pressure on the euro; a defeat would add to it. Britain's budget next week is the next fiscal test after that.

fed.summary: The Fed is expected to hold in October and is likely to hike in December. US yields stayed high overnight, which keeps the dollar supported while it waits.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely (about 4 in 5).
fed.why: Inflation ran hot last week and oil keeps pushing yields up. Weak housing is a reason for caution, but not enough to change the plan.
fed.watch: The Fed is in its quiet period until the October 28 decision. Until then, oil and US yields set the tone.

boc.summary: Markets now expect the Bank of Canada to hike on October 28 after Macklem warned oil will push inflation up. That shift has lifted the loonie.
boc.why: Macklem said the bank will raise its inflation forecast sharply and must act on where inflation is heading, not on today's cool core prices. Several big Canadian banks changed their calls to a hike.
boc.watch: Oil prices, and whether any BoC official pushes back on hike bets before the October 28 decision.

rbnz.summary: Markets now lean firmly toward an RBNZ hike on October 28. A rise in rates would support the kiwi, but Wednesday's inflation report has to back it up.
rbnz.why: Strong business activity and the bank's own signal that rates are more likely to go up are driving the hike bets. A wide trade gap is the main argument for waiting.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's inflation figure on Wednesday. A soft number would put a hold back on the table.

ecb.summary: The ECB is expected to hold in October and lean toward a December hike. France's unrest is weighing on the euro more than rate hopes are helping it.
ecb.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Inflation is near a three-year high, and German factory prices just jumped again, so a December hike is still the base case. French bond stress is the main worry.
ecb.watch: France's budget vote on Tuesday, Lagarde on Wednesday and Moody's review of France on Friday.

boj.summary: The BoJ is signalling more hikes, most likely in December rather than October. Until then the yen stays weak because US rates are so much higher.
boj.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Ueda said underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal. But inflation is still below the bank's own forecast, so there is no rush.
boj.watch: Japan's inflation report on Friday and the bank's new forecasts on October 30. Also the yen near 160 per dollar.

rba.summary: The RBA hints rates may not be high enough yet, keeping a November hike possible. The Aussie is leaning more on China and risk mood than on the RBA right now.
rba.priced: November: hike about 1 in 3; December: a coin flip.
rba.why: Kent said the neutral rate may be rising and inflation is stuck. He also said the job market is loosening faster than expected.
rba.watch: Deputy Governor Hauser speaks Tuesday evening, then Australia's quarterly inflation report on October 28.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, and a surprise drop in unemployment made that firmer. The pound rose on the news.
boe.priced: November 5: hike almost fully expected; December an open question.
boe.why: Unemployment fell and regular pay growth edged up, so wage pressure is not fading. Inflation is expected to rise again too.
boe.watch: UK inflation on Wednesday and Bailey's speech the same day. A hot number would bring a December hike into play.

snb.summary: The SNB holds at zero and could cut in December because Swiss inflation is very low. The franc moves on outside fear and stays near its strongest against the euro in three months.
snb.priced: Holding at 0%; a December cut is possible.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is very soft, so the bank has no reason to tighten. The franc's moves come from France and the Middle East, not Swiss news.
snb.watch: Thursday's write-up of the SNB's last meeting. More European or Gulf stress would lift the franc regardless.
